# 2 Kings Chapter 16 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 237r–237v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_016_page_472.jpg, 2KI_016_page_473.jpg

---

**1** In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah's reign in Israel, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah.

**2** Ahaz was twenty when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. Unlike his ancestor David, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God.

**3** Instead, he followed the ways of the kings of Israel. He even sacrificed his own son in the fire, imitating the detestable practices of the nations the LORD had driven out to make room for Israel.

**4** He offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places, on the hilltops, and under every spreading tree.

**5** Then King Rezin of Aram and King Pekah of Israel marched up to attack Jerusalem. They besieged Ahaz but could not defeat him.

**6** Around the same time, King Rezin of Aram recaptured Elath for Aram, expelling the Judeans. Aramean settlers moved in and have lived there ever since.

**7** Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria with this appeal: "I am your loyal servant — your son. Come and rescue me from the kings of Aram and Israel, who are attacking me."

**8** To back up his plea, Ahaz took the silver and gold from the LORD's temple and from the royal treasury and sent it all as a payment to the Assyrian king.

**9** The king of Assyria agreed. He marched against Damascus, captured it, deported its population to Kir, and executed Rezin.

**10** King Ahaz then traveled to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser. While there, he saw an altar that impressed him. He sent Uriah the priest a detailed sketch and a complete set of dimensions for the altar.

**11** Uriah built a replica of it. He had it finished by the time Ahaz returned from Damascus.

**12** When the king arrived and saw the altar, he approached it and made offerings on it personally.

**13** He burned his burnt offering and grain offering, poured out his drink offering, and splashed the blood of his fellowship offerings against the altar.

**14** As for the original bronze altar that stood before the LORD, he moved it away from the front of the temple — from its position between the new altar and the LORD's house — and placed it off to the north side.

**15** Then King Ahaz gave Uriah the priest these orders: "Use the large new altar for the morning burnt offering, the evening grain offering, the royal offerings, and the offerings of all the people — their grain offerings, drink offerings, and all the blood from burnt offerings and sacrifices. Splash all of it on this altar. As for the bronze altar — I will use that for seeking guidance."

**16** Uriah the priest carried out everything the king ordered.

**17** Ahaz then stripped the decorative panels from the bronze stands and removed the basins from them. He took the great Sea down from the bronze oxen that supported it and set it on a stone platform instead.

**18** He also dismantled the covered Sabbath walkway that had been built at the temple, along with the king's outer entrance, removing them from the LORD's house — all to appease the king of Assyria.

**19** The rest of the events of Ahaz's reign are recorded in the court annals of the kings of Judah.

**20** Ahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Hezekiah succeeded him as king.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 3 — "sacrificed his own son in the fire":** This is the point of no return for Ahaz — and a turning point for Judah. The phrase "passed through the fire" is the biblical euphemism for child sacrifice. The narrator makes sure we feel the horror: Ahaz does exactly what the Canaanites did, the very thing that caused God to hand them over to Israel. The king of God's people has become the thing God destroyed.

**Verse 7 — "I am your servant — your son":** This is more than politics. In the ancient Near East, calling yourself someone's "son" meant pledging total loyalty. Ahaz, king of the people who called God their Father, transfers that filial relationship to a foreign emperor. It is theological treason wrapped in diplomatic language.

**Verse 10 — The altar copy:** There is bitter irony in this scene. When Moses was on the mountain, God gave him the pattern for the tabernacle. When Ahaz is in Damascus, he copies a pagan altar and sends the blueprint home. He is an anti-Moses: receiving foreign religion instead of divine revelation.

**Verse 17-18 — Dismantling the temple:** Ahaz systematically undoes Solomon's work. The panels, the Sea, the oxen, the Sabbath structures — each item Solomon carefully designed and installed, Ahaz removes or degrades. Every change is made "because of the king of Assyria" — the refrain of a king who has replaced YHWH with an empire.

*— PNEUMA*
